questions.prompt: A signal \(\cos(\omega t)\) passes through a square-law nonlinearity. Using \(\cos^2(\omega t)=\tfrac12\left(1+\cos 2\omega t\right)\), which frequencies appear at the output?
questions.explanation: Reader Eq. 18.30. Squaring a sinusoid creates a DC term \(\tfrac12\) and a second harmonic \(\tfrac12\cos2\omega t\). A real amplifier with \(a_1v+a_2v^2\) therefore outputs the fundamental (from \(a_1\)) plus DC and \(2\omega\) (from \(a_2\)).

questions.prompt: Op-amp datasheets quote input voltage noise in \(\mathrm{nV/\sqrt{Hz}}\). How do you get the RMS noise voltage over a bandwidth \(B\) (white noise)?
options: The density already is the RMS voltage
questions.explanation: The noise POWER per hertz is \(e_n^2\) (in \(\mathrm{V^2/Hz}\)); for a flat spectrum the power in \(B\) is \(e_n^2B\), and the RMS voltage is \(e_n\sqrt B\) (reader Sec. 18.5.2). That's why the unit has a square root of hertz.

questions.prompt: What is the RMS thermal noise voltage of a \(10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) resistor at 300 K in a 100 kHz bandwidth, \(v_R=\sqrt{4kTR\Delta f}\), in µV? (\(k=1.381\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J/K}\))
questions.explanation:
\(4kTR\Delta f=4(1.381\times10^{-23})(300)(10^4)(10^5)=1.657\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{V^2}\); square root \(=4.07\ \mu\mathrm{V}\) (reader Eq. 18.35).
Rule-of-thumb check: 1 kΩ in 1 MHz ≈ 4 µV; 10× the resistance and 1/10 the bandwidth gives the same \(R\Delta f\), so ≈ 4 µV ✔.

questions.prompt: An amplifier has \(v_o=a_1v_i+a_3v_i^3\) with \(a_1=1\) and \(a_3=0.1\ \mathrm{V^{-2}}\). For \(v_i=1\ \mathrm{V}\cdot\cos\omega t\), what is the third-harmonic amplitude as a percentage of the fundamental? Use \(\cos^3x=\tfrac34\cos x+\tfrac14\cos3x\).
questions.explanation:
\(a_3\cos^3\omega t=0.1\left(\tfrac34\cos\omega t+\tfrac14\cos3\omega t\right)\) (reader Eq. 18.33).
Fundamental: \(1+0.075=1.075\). Third harmonic: \(0.025\). Ratio \(=2.326\%\).
Common mistake: forgetting that the cubic term also adds to the fundamental (giving 2.5%).
questions.figure_alt: S-shaped transfer curve that compresses at large inputs.

questions.prompt: How does op-amp noise differ from offset voltage?
options: Noise is a fixed DC value; offset is random AC
Noise is a random AC signal described by its spectral density (and RMS value); offset is a fixed DC value for a given part
Noise only appears at the output, offset only at the input
questions.explanation: Both are modeled as sources at the input of an ideal op-amp (reader Fig. 18.21 and 18.1), but offset is a constant (random only across parts), while noise fluctuates in time with a flat ('white') spectrum, so it's specified per root hertz and integrated over bandwidth.

questions.prompt: Two uncorrelated noise sources contribute 3 µV RMS and 4 µV RMS at the same node. What is the total RMS noise?
questions.explanation: Uncorrelated random signals add in POWER (mean-square): \(v^2=3^2+4^2=25\ \mu\mathrm{V^2}\), so 5 µV RMS. Adding RMS values directly would only hold for perfectly correlated (identical) signals.

questions.prompt: An amplifier with \(e_n=20\ \mathrm{nV/\sqrt{Hz}}\) (white) is followed by an ideal band-pass filter from 10 kHz to 100 kHz. What is the RMS noise, in µV?
questions.explanation:
The noise bandwidth is the WIDTH of the band, \(100-10=90\ \mathrm{kHz}\), not 100 kHz: \(20\ \mathrm{nV}\times\sqrt{90\,000}=6\ \mu\mathrm{V}\).
Using 100 kHz would give 6.32 µV.

questions.prompt: An amplifier's transfer curve is odd-symmetric, \(v_o(-v_i)=-v_o(v_i)\), like the S-curve shown. Driven by a pure sine, which harmonics can appear?
options: No harmonics, since the curve is symmetric
questions.explanation: An odd function has only odd powers in its Taylor series (\(a_1v+a_3v^3+a_5v^5\dots\)), and odd powers of \(\cos\) contain only odd harmonics (Eq. 18.33). Even harmonics come from even powers like \(v^2\), which an odd-symmetric curve lacks. Differential (balanced) circuits use this to cancel even-order distortion.

questions.prompt: Preview of datasheets. A 10 mV RMS audio signal is amplified by an op-amp with \(e_n=10\ \mathrm{nV/\sqrt{Hz}}\) over a 20 kHz bandwidth. Considering only that noise, what is the SNR at the input, in dB?
questions.explanation:
Noise \(=10\ \mathrm{nV}\times\sqrt{20\,000}=1.414\ \mu\mathrm{V}\). \(SNR=20\log_{10}\dfrac{10\ \mathrm{mV}}{1.414\ \mu\mathrm{V}}=76.99\ \mathrm{dB}\).
Datasheet noise specs let you predict SNR before building anything.

questions.prompt: Preview of datasheets. A gain-100 non-inverting amplifier uses an op-amp with \(e_n=5\ \mathrm{nV/\sqrt{Hz}}\) and \(f_u=10\ \mathrm{MHz}\). Treat the closed-loop bandwidth \(f_u/100\) as a brick wall. What RMS noise appears at the output, in µV?
questions.explanation:
Bandwidth \(=100\ \mathrm{kHz}\). Input noise \(=5\ \mathrm{nV}\times\sqrt{10^5}=1.58\ \mu\mathrm{V}\). The input noise source is amplified like a signal at the \(+\) input: \(\times100\Rightarrow158.1\ \mu\mathrm{V}\) RMS.
(Real single-pole roll-off adds a factor \(\pi/2\) to the noise bandwidth, a refinement for later.)

questions.prompt: Preview of datasheets. An op-amp stage has 1% distortion open-loop. Wrapped in feedback with loop gain \(T=99\) and compared at the same output amplitude, about how much distortion remains (this is how datasheet THD figures are measured)?
questions.explanation: Distortion generated inside the loop is reduced by \(1+T=100\) at equal output level (the noise-rejection result from the loop-gain skill): \(1\%/100=0.01\%\). This is why the reader says harmonics are tiny in negative-feedback circuits.
